summary: Not Enough Space is our team's response to the challenge of telling the story of NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. We were struck by how much real hardware NASA has left across the solar system, and how little of that story reaches children. The data exists in NASA's NSSDCA archive, but it is written for engineers, while most space content for kids is cartoonish or missing entirely. So we built a free, offline web app that meets young learners where they are. A child reads a short comic, then dives to "fish" real artifacts out of orbit, collects them into a museum, and earns a certificate with their own explorer name. Every artifact links back to its live NSSDCA record, keeping the story tied to real science. The app is bilingual (English/Spanish) and built for accessibility from the start, with keyboard and screen-reader support, high contrast, reduced motion, and text-to-speech. No account, no ads, no paywall, just rigorous NASA data made welcoming for the next generation of space enthusiasts.
details:
Not Enough Space is a free, browser-based educational game that turns NASA's abandoned hardware, the rovers, landers, and probes left across the Moon, Mars, and deep space, into something a child actually wants to explore. We built it as a Progressive Web App, so it installs to a tablet or laptop like any app and keeps working without internet. There is no account, no advertising, and no paywall: you open the page and play.

How it works. The experience is a four-step loop. Read: a short comic chapter gives a piece of discarded equipment a voice and tells the human story behind it. We wrote fourteen chapters in total, five on the Moon, six on Mars, and three in deep space. Dive: a "Deep Space Dive" mini-game where the child fishes the abandoned hardware out of the depths of space by answering simple questions. The dive depth is driven by real NSSDCA data such as orbit altitude and distance from Earth, so play and data become the same thing. Collect: every recovered artifact lands in a Space Junk Museum and a personal Collection Album, each showing its real name, location, and a link back to its NSSDCA record. Earn: a personalized Explorer Certificate rewards progress and gives teachers and parents a tangible takeaway.

Benefits and impact. Every artifact is grounded in the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), the exact data source the challenge points to, and each one links back to its source. The app is bilingual, English and Spanish, and accessibility-first by design: full keyboard navigation, screen-reader support through ARIA labels, high-contrast and easy-read modes, text scaling, reduced-motion, and optional text-to-speech. Because it is an offline PWA, a teacher in a low-bandwidth classroom can install it once and use it for years. The intended impact is straightforward: a seven-year-old finishes a chapter in five minutes and comes away knowing that Spirit and Opportunity are real robots still sitting on Mars, turning passive scrolling into genuine STEM curiosity.

Tools and development. We built the app with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as a no-build PWA, with a service worker for offline use and a manifest for installability. No external libraries or frameworks load at runtime, and the typeface is self-hosted so the whole experience works offline. We drew directly on NASA's NSSDCA archive for artifact data, with age-appropriate framing from NASA Space Place and supplementary context from Krillion.

Creativity and design choices. Our core idea is a new metaphor: instead of a static gallery, the child retrieves abandoned equipment by fishing it out of orbit, and the depth they reach reflects real orbital data. We gave the hardware a voice, with chapters titled things like "The Grave of the Innocent Scouts" and "The Long Goodbye," so the storytelling respects children's curiosity rather than talking down to them. Above all we optimized for zero-friction reach, so the product meets children on their own devices and in their own language.
dataRefs: NSSDCA — NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive
